title: Working with AI tools
summary: Validating model output, modelling tool calls and reviewing generated code.

lessons.title: Structured output
lessons.body:
# Structured output

A language model returns text. To use a reply in a program, you ask for JSON and then treat that reply as untrusted input, the same way you would treat a form submission.

Replies go wrong in predictable ways:

- The JSON is wrapped in a code fence, with a sentence around it.
- A field is missing, or has the wrong type.
- A number arrives as a string, or falls outside the allowed range.
- There are extra fields you did not ask for.

So parse first, then check every field, and report all the problems at once. That message can go back to the model for another attempt.

```python
import json

data = json.loads('{"score": 3}')
if not isinstance(data, dict):
    raise ValueError("not an object")
```

Note that `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `isinstance(True, int)` is true. Test for it separately when you need a real number.
lessons.task: Write `parse_reply(text)`. Strip one optional code fence, parse the JSON, and return only `title` (non-empty string), `priority` (int from 1 to 5, not a bool) and `tags` (list of strings, default `[]`). Otherwise raise `ValueError` naming every invalid field.

checks.name: tags are optional, extras are dropped
strips a code fence
checks.code:
fence = "`" * 3
got = parse_reply(fence + 'json
{"title": "Fix", "priority": 1}
' + fence + "
")
assert got == {"title": "Fix", "priority": 1, "tags": []}, got

checks.name: rejects invalid JSON and non-objects
rejects bad field values
checks.code:
bad = [
    '{"priority": 1}',
    '{"title": "", "priority": 1}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": 0}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": 6}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": "3"}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": true}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": 1, "tags": "a"}',
    '{"title": "x", "priority": 1, "tags": [1]}',
]
for text in bad:
    raised = False
    try:
        parse_reply(text)
    except ValueError:
        raised = True
    assert raised, f"{text} should raise ValueError"

checks.name: names every invalid field

hints: Handle the fence first: if the stripped text starts with three backticks, drop the first and last lines. `json.JSONDecodeError` is already a `ValueError`.
Collect problem names in a list, and raise only after checking all three fields. `type(priority) is not int` rejects both `bool` and `float`.

Check `title` with `isinstance` and emptiness, `priority` with `type(...) is int` and `1 <= priority <= 5`, and `tags` with `data.get("tags", [])` and `all(isinstance(t, str) for t in tags)`. Then return a new dict with just those keys.
lessons.explanation:
Returning a new dict means extra fields cannot slip into later code. Validation libraries such as pydantic do this for larger schemas, and the idea is the same.

Reporting every problem in one message gives the model enough information to fix its reply in a single retry, instead of one field per attempt. API features that constrain output to a schema reduce these errors, but your program should still validate.

lessons.title: Tool calling
lessons.body:
# Tool calling

A model cannot run anything itself. With tool calling, it replies with a structured request, your code performs the call, and you send the result back. The loop repeats until the model answers in plain text.

A request is just data:

```python
call = {
    "name": "add",
    "arguments": {"a": 2, "b": 3},
}
```

The safe way to run it is a dispatch table: a dict of the functions you allow.

```python
TOOLS = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b}
fn = TOOLS[call["name"]]
print(fn(**call["arguments"]))  # 5
```

## Rules

- The name is untrusted. Look it up in the table, and never pass it to `eval` or `getattr`.
- Arguments may be wrong or missing.
- A failing tool must not crash the loop. Return the error as data, so the model can read it and try again.
lessons.task: Write `TOOLS` with `add(a, b)` and `word_count(text)`. Write `run_tool_call(call, tools=TOOLS)` returning `{"ok": True, "result": value}` on success and `{"ok": False, "error": message}` for a call that is not a dict, an unknown or missing name, non-dict arguments, wrong arguments, or a tool that raises. Missing `arguments` means `{}`.

checks.name: runs the built-in tools
checks.code:
got = run_tool_call({"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 2, "b": 3}})
assert got == {"ok": True, "result": 5}, got
got = run_tool_call({"name": "word_count", "arguments": {"text": "one two three"}})
assert got == {"ok": True, "result": 3}, got

checks.name: unknown names are refused
malformed calls do not crash
wrong arguments become errors
checks.code:
got = run_tool_call({"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1}})
assert got["ok"] is False and "error" in got, got
got = run_tool_call({"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}})
assert got["ok"] is False and "error" in got, got

checks.name: a failing tool becomes an error
checks.code:
def boom():
    raise RuntimeError("disk full")
got = run_tool_call({"name": "boom"}, tools={"boom": boom})
assert got["ok"] is False and "disk full" in got["error"], got

checks.name: uses the table it is given
checks.code:
got = run_tool_call({"name": "ping"}, tools={"ping": lambda: "pong"})
assert got == {"ok": True, "result": "pong"}, got
got = run_tool_call({"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}, tools={})
assert got["ok"] is False, got

hints: Validate in order: is the call a dict, is the name a string in the table, are the arguments a dict. Each failure returns an error dict.
The name might be a list, which is unhashable, so `name in tools` would raise. Test that it is a string first.
`tools[name](**arguments)` inside `try`, with `except Exception as error:` returning `{"ok": False, "error": f"{type(error).__name__}: {error}"}`.
lessons.explanation:
The table is a list of what is allowed. Anything absent cannot run, however the name is spelled, which is the property you want when the name comes from a model.

`except Exception` is broad on purpose here. This is a boundary where every tool failure must turn into a result the loop can return. Bad arguments surface as `TypeError` from the `**arguments` call, so they need no separate code.

lessons.title: Reviewing AI-written code
lessons.body:
# Reviewing AI-written code

Generated code tends to look finished, so read it as you would a stranger's pull request. Run it on awkward inputs before you trust it.

## What to look for

- State that outlives a call, such as a mutable default argument.
- Float arithmetic on money or other exact quantities.
- Off-by-one errors at boundaries and in paging.
- `except` blocks that swallow failures and hide bad data.
- Calls to functions that do not exist. Check names against the documentation.
- Tests that assert what the code does, rather than what it should do.

```python
print(int(4.35 * 100))    # 434
print(round(4.35 * 100))  # 435
```

The first line looks reasonable, and its answer is still wrong.

## Review by trying

Write down what each function should do for empty input, for one item, and for bad input. Call it with those. Do not accept a fix you cannot explain.
lessons.task: An assistant wrote these three functions, and each has at least one bug. `normalize_emails` should trim and lower-case, skip blanks, and drop duplicates within one call. `page_of` should return a 1-based page and raise `ValueError` for a page below 1. `total_cents` should sum decimal price strings exactly and raise `ValueError` on a bad price. Fix them.

checks.name: emails are cleaned
checks.code:
got = normalize_emails([" A@x.io ", "", "   ", "b@x.io", "a@X.io"])
assert got == ["a@x.io", "b@x.io"], got

checks.name: no memory between calls
checks.code:
first = normalize_emails(["a@x.io"])
second = normalize_emails(["a@x.io"])
assert first == ["a@x.io"], first
assert second == ["a@x.io"], second

checks.name: pages start at 1
checks.code:
items = list(range(1, 8))
assert page_of(items, 1, 3) == [1, 2, 3], page_of(items, 1, 3)
assert page_of(items, 3, 3) == [7], page_of(items, 3, 3)
assert page_of(items, 4, 3) == [], page_of(items, 4, 3)

checks.name: page below 1 raises
prices are exact
checks.code:
assert total_cents(["4.35"]) == 435, total_cents(["4.35"])
assert total_cents(["0.07", "0.57", "1.10"]) == 174, total_cents(["0.07", "0.57", "1.10"])
assert total_cents([]) == 0, total_cents([])

checks.name: bad prices raise

hints: Call each function twice with awkward input and compare with the description. `normalize_emails(["a@x.io"])` twice is a good start.
Three things to look at: `seen=[]` survives between calls, `page * size` skips the first page, and `float` cannot hold `4.35` exactly.

Create `seen` inside the function and use `email.strip().lower()`. Use `start = (page - 1) * size` after a range check. Add `Decimal(price)` values, catching `decimal.InvalidOperation` and raising `ValueError`, then `int(total * 100)`.
lessons.explanation:
Each bug passed casual testing. The default list only misbehaves on the second call, the page bug only shows on the first page, and the float bug depends on which price you try.

`Decimal` built from a string holds the exact value you read, so `Decimal("4.35") * 100` is exactly `435`. The original `except ... pass` also meant bad prices shrank the total with no warning, which is worse than a crash because nobody notices.
